lessons.title: Hello and Goodbye
audioSourceTexts: Notice the stress in GOOD MORning and good EVEning.
Repeat short greetings without adding an extra vowel at the end.
Good morning! I'm Sarah. Nice to meet you. — Hi, Sarah! I'm Daniel. Nice to meet you too. — Goodbye, Daniel. — Goodbye!
Say three greetings aloud: one for morning, one for afternoon and one for evening.

lessons.title: My Name Is…
audioSourceTexts: I'm is one beat: /aɪm/.
What's your… often connects naturally in speech.
Hi! What's your name? — I'm Maria. What's your name? — My name is Alex. — Nice to meet you, Alex. — Nice to meet you too.
Record or say: 'Hello. I'm ____. Nice to meet you.'

lessons.title: Alphabet and Spelling
audioSourceTexts: Focus on easily confused letters: A/E/I, G/J, M/N, B/V.
Practise your own name slowly, then at natural speed.
My name is Mia. That's M-I-A. My last name is Costa: C-O-S-T-A.
Spell your first name, last name and your city aloud.

lessons.title: Numbers, Age and Phone Numbers
audioSourceTexts: Contrast THIRteen / THIRty and FOURteen / FORty.
Say phone numbers in small groups with short pauses.
I'm twenty-four years old. My phone number is zero nine one, five five two, eight four six.
Say your age and a fictional phone number slowly and clearly.

lessons.title: Countries and Nationalities
audioSourceTexts: Brazilian: stress on ZIL: bra-ZIL-ian.
Portuguese: stress on GUESE: Portu-GUESE.
I'm Clara. I'm from Portugal, but I live in France. I'm Portuguese. My friend Leo is from Brazil. He's Brazilian.
Introduce yourself with your name, age, country, nationality and language.

lessons.title: Checkpoint — First Conversation
audioSourceTexts: Use clear rhythm; don't try to speak too fast.
Good afternoon! I'm Emma. What's your name? — I'm Rafael. — How do you spell that? — R-A-F-A-E-L. — Nice to meet you. Where are you from? — I'm from Brazil. I'm Brazilian. — Nice to meet you, Rafael.
Final mission: have a complete first conversation using greeting, name, spelling, age and origin.

lessons.title: My Family
audioSourceTexts: mother / father: notice the voiced TH /ð/.
family often sounds like three syllables: FAM-i-ly.
This is my family. Maria is my mother and Carlos is my father. I have one brother, Lucas, and one sister, Sofia.
Describe four people in your family or an imaginary family.

lessons.title: Jobs and People
audioSourceTexts: Use an before vowel sounds: an engineer.
Stress the first syllable in TEAcher, DOCtor, DRIver.
I'm Nina. I'm a nurse. My husband, Tom, is an engineer. My sister is a teacher and my brother is a student.
Say what you do and name the jobs of two people you know.

lessons.title: Have and Has
audioSourceTexts: has ends with /z/: /hæz/.
don't and doesn't are normally unstressed in natural sentences.
I have a small car and a bike. My sister has a dog, but she doesn't have a car. My parents have two cats.
Make five true or fictional sentences with have/has.

lessons.title: This, That, These, Those
audioSourceTexts: this/these begin with /ð/.
Listen to the vowel contrast: this / these.
This is my phone here. That is your bag over there. These are my keys, and those are your glasses.
Point to four objects and make one sentence with this, that, these and those.

lessons.title: Whose Is It?
audioSourceTexts: his usually starts with a clear /h/ in careful speech.
Whose sounds like 'who's' but has a different meaning.
This is Anna. Her hair is dark and she's tall. This is her brother Ben. His hair is short. Their dog is very friendly.
Describe two people and two things they own.

lessons.title: Checkpoint — Meet My People
audioSourceTexts: Review /ð/ in mother, this, these.
Keep sentences short and clear.
This is my sister Julia. She's a teacher. She has a small car and a dog. Her dog is called Max. Those are her glasses on the table.
Final mission: introduce an imaginary family of at least four people, with jobs, one possession and one adjective each.

lessons.title: From Morning to Night
audioSourceTexts: Practise linking in 'go_to work' and 'go_to bed'.
Keep wake up and get up as two-word chunks.
I wake up at seven, have breakfast, and go to work at eight. I have lunch at one. In the evening, I study English and go to bed at eleven.
Tell your morning routine using at least four actions.

lessons.title: Time and Days
audioSourceTexts: Wednesday has fewer sounds than its spelling suggests.
Stress SATurday and SUNday.
My English class is on Tuesday at half past seven. On Thursday it starts at eight o'clock.
Say your schedule for three days of the week with times.

lessons.title: Simple Present
audioSourceTexts: Final -s can sound /s/, /z/ or /ɪz/.
works /s/, lives /z/, finishes /ɪz/.
Leo lives in Porto. He works in a hotel. He starts at nine and finishes at five. In the evening, he cooks and watches TV.
Describe one person's routine using five he/she sentences.

lessons.title: Do You…?
audioSourceTexts: Does often has a weak vowel in natural speech.
After does/doesn't, use base verb: work, not works.
Do you work at weekends? — No, I don't. I work Monday to Friday. Does your sister work? — Yes, she does. She works in a shop.
Ask yourself five routine questions and answer them aloud.

lessons.title: Always, Usually, Sometimes, Never
audioSourceTexts: Usually often reduces to about three syllables in fast speech.
Stress the frequency word when contrasting habits.
I usually get up at seven. I always have coffee. I sometimes walk to work, but I never walk when it rains.
Make six true sentences about your routine using frequency words.

lessons.title: Checkpoint — My Day
audioSourceTexts: Review third-person -s and linking.
Aim for clear chunks, not speed.
Maya gets up at six thirty. She usually has breakfast at seven. She works from eight to four. She never works on Sunday. In the evening she often reads or watches a film.
Final mission: describe your day from morning to night and answer five follow-up questions.

lessons.title: Rooms and Furniture
audioSourceTexts: Kitchen: /ˈkɪtʃən/.
Bedroom: stress BED-room.
My flat has a living room, a kitchen, one bedroom and one bathroom. The sofa is in the living room. The table is in the kitchen.
Name the rooms in your home and one object in each room.

lessons.title: There Is / There Are
audioSourceTexts: There's is a common contraction of there is.
Avoid saying 'there are' too slowly; practise it as one chunk.
There is a sofa in the living room. There are two chairs and a small table. There is a lamp next to the sofa. There are three pictures on the wall.
Describe a room with at least three 'There is/are' sentences.

lessons.title: Where Is It?
audioSourceTexts: Link next_to naturally.
Front of often connects in speech: front_of.
The phone is on the table. The keys are in the bag under the chair. The lamp is next to the sofa.
Use a room around you and describe five object positions.

lessons.title: Places in Town
audioSourceTexts: Hospital stress: HOS-pi-tal.
Restaurant may have fewer syllables than Portuguese speakers expect.
The station is in the centre. The hotel is next to the station. The pharmacy is across from the supermarket. The park is behind the museum.
Say where you go for food, medicine, transport and money.

lessons.title: Basic Directions
audioSourceTexts: right ends in /t/.
Practise turn_right and go_straight as chunks.
Go straight for one block. Turn left at the bank. Go past the supermarket. The pharmacy is on your right.
Give directions from an imaginary station to a pharmacy using three steps.

lessons.title: Checkpoint — My Neighbourhood
audioSourceTexts: Review connected chunks: next_to, go_straight, turn_left.
There is a small park near my house. The supermarket is next to the park. To get to the pharmacy, go straight, turn right at the bank, and the pharmacy is on the left.
Final mission: describe one room and then guide someone from your home to a place in your neighbourhood.

lessons.title: Food and Drinks
audioSourceTexts: water differs by accent; keep the first syllable strong.
coffee stress: COF-fee.
For breakfast I have coffee, bread and cheese. I like bananas, but I don't like apples very much. For lunch I usually have chicken, rice and salad.
Say five foods/drinks you like and two you don't like.

lessons.title: Countable and Uncountable
audioSourceTexts: an links to a following vowel sound: an_apple.
Plural -s: eggs /z/, apples /z/.
We need two apples, three eggs, some bread, some rice and some water.
Look at a kitchen list and say quantities for six items.

lessons.title: Some, Any, Much, Many
audioSourceTexts: any: /ˈeni/.
many and much are stressed when contrasting quantities.
Do we have any milk? — Yes, we have some. How many eggs do we have? — Six. How much water do we need? — Two bottles.
Ask and answer four kitchen quantity questions.

lessons.title: Prices and Shopping
audioSourceTexts: thirty vs thirteen is important for prices.
euro/euros: keep the initial 'y' sound in careful English.
How much is this T-shirt? — It's twenty-five euros. — Do you have it in medium? — Yes, in blue and black. — Great. I'll take the blue one.
Role-play buying a T-shirt: ask price, size and colour, then buy or refuse.

lessons.title: At a Café
audioSourceTexts: I'd like = /aɪd laɪk/.
Can I have…? often links: can_I_have.
Hi. I'd like a coffee and a cheese sandwich, please. — Anything else? — Yes, some water, please. — Of course. — That's all, thank you.
Role-play a café order with at least two items and ask for the bill.

lessons.title: Checkpoint — Café and Shop
audioSourceTexts: Review numbers/prices and polite sentence rhythm.
Customer: I'd like two bottles of water and a sandwich, please. Assistant: That's eight euros fifty. Customer: Can I pay by card? Assistant: Yes, of course.
Final mission: buy one clothing item, then order food and a drink at a café.

lessons.title: Actions Now
audioSourceTexts: -ing normally ends /ɪŋ/, not /in/.
Practise walking, talking, working as whole words.
Look at the park. A man is running. Two women are talking. A child is eating an ice cream, and a dog is sleeping under a tree.
Look around and say three things people are doing now.

lessons.title: Present Continuous
audioSourceTexts: Use contractions naturally: I'm, he's, she's, we're, they're.
Don't drop the verb be.
I'm studying English. My sister is cooking. My parents are watching TV. Our dog is sleeping.
Describe what four people in an imaginary house are doing right now.

lessons.title: What Are You Doing?
audioSourceTexts: What are you…? often connects naturally.
Isn't and aren't are useful negative contractions.
What are you doing? — I'm waiting for the bus. Is Sara with you? — No, she isn't. She's working today.
Ask and answer five 'What are… doing?' questions using a picture or imagination.

lessons.title: Clothes
audioSourceTexts: clothes: the ending is compact; don't overpronounce.
shirt vs T-shirt: stress T in T-shirt.
Anna is wearing a red dress and black shoes. Ben is wearing jeans, a white T-shirt and a blue jacket.
Describe what you are wearing now, then describe another person in a picture.

lessons.title: Weather Today
audioSourceTexts: weather begins with voiced /ð/.
windy stress: WIN-dy.
It's cold and rainy today. People are wearing jackets. One woman is waiting for a bus under an umbrella. Two children are running to a café.
Describe today's weather and say what you are wearing/doing because of it.

lessons.title: Checkpoint — What's Happening?
audioSourceTexts: Review contractions and -ing.
It's sunny in the park. A man is reading on a bench. Two children are playing. A woman is wearing a yellow dress and taking a photo. A dog is running near the trees.
Final mission: speak for 60–90 seconds describing a busy picture without reading.

lessons.title: Can and Can't
audioSourceTexts: can is often weak in affirmative sentences.
can't is stressed more strongly.
I can swim and ride a bike, but I can't drive. My friend Zoe can drive and cook very well, but she can't swim.
Say five things you can do and two things you can't do yet.

lessons.title: Can I…? Can You…?
audioSourceTexts: Can I links naturally: can_I.
Can you often sounds like one smooth chunk.
Excuse me, can you help me? — Of course. — Can I use this chair? — Yes, no problem. — Thank you.
Make four polite requests: two with Can I and two with Can you.

lessons.title: Signs and Instructions
audioSourceTexts: Imperatives often have strong first words: STOP, WAIT, TURN.
Don't enter: connect the two words naturally.
Please wait here. Don't enter this room. Turn off your phone and keep left in the corridor.
Read five common signs aloud and explain them in simple Portuguese or English.

lessons.title: Getting Around
audioSourceTexts: by bus / by train: keep 'by' short.
ticket stress: TICK-et.
I usually go to work by bus. The bus stop is near my house. On Saturdays I walk to the centre. My friend goes everywhere by bike.
Explain how you normally travel to work/study and how you travel on weekends.

lessons.title: Asking for Directions
audioSourceTexts: Excuse me: stress the second word slightly.
How do I get to…? practised as one chunk.
Excuse me, how do I get to the station? — Go straight, turn left at the traffic lights, and it's next to the hotel. — Is it far? — No, about five minutes.
Role-play asking for directions, including one clarification request.

lessons.title: Checkpoint — Can You Help Me?
audioSourceTexts: Review can/can't contrast and route chunks.
Excuse me, can you help me? I need to get to the hospital. — Of course. Take bus 12 from this stop. Get off at King Street, then go straight. The hospital is on your right. — Thank you!
Final mission: ask for help, choose transport and repeat a three-step route.

lessons.title: At a Hotel
audioSourceTexts: reservation stress: reser-VA-tion.
room has a long vowel in many accents.
Hello, I have a reservation. My name is Sofia Costa. — Yes, room 204. Breakfast is from seven to ten. The lift is on your left. — Thank you.
Role-play hotel check-in, then ask about breakfast and Wi-Fi.

lessons.title: At a Restaurant
audioSourceTexts: vegetarian stress: vege-TAIR-ian.
dessert has stress on the second syllable.
A table for two, please. — Of course. — I'd like the chicken and rice. My friend would like the vegetarian pasta. Can we have some water too?
Role-play entering a restaurant, ordering a main dish and drink, then asking for the bill.

lessons.title: Buying Clothes
audioSourceTexts: fits ends /ts/.
try_on links naturally.
Can I try this jacket on? — Of course. The changing room is over there. — It's too big. Do you have a smaller size? — Yes, here's a medium.
Role-play trying on a jacket and asking for another size/colour.

lessons.title: Basic Health and Emergencies
audioSourceTexts: headache stress: HEAD-ache.
stomach: STUM-ək.
I don't feel well. I have a bad headache and my stomach hurts. — Do you need a doctor? — Yes, please.
Practise saying one symptom and asking where the nearest pharmacy/doctor is.

lessons.title: Messages and Small Talk
audioSourceTexts: email stress: E-mail.
How are you? often reduces naturally but keep it clear.
Hi, can I leave a message for Emma? Please tell her Rafael called. My number is 091 555 204. Ask her to call me later. Thank you.
Leave a 20-second fictional phone message with your name, number and request.

lessons.title: A1 Final Mission
audioSourceTexts: Prioritise intelligibility, chunking and confidence over speed.

Welcome to the A1 final mission. First, introduce yourself. Then imagine you are visiting a new city: check in at a hotel, ask how to get to a café, order a drink and snack, and leave a short message for a friend.
Capstone: 4–6 minute guided simulation covering introduction, routine, hotel, directions, café and a short message.

lessons.title: Yesterday's Story

weak pronunciation of did in questions
clear contrast was / were

A: How was your weekend?
B: Pretty good, actually. I went to Bristol with my sister.
A: Really? What did you do there?
B: We visited a museum in the morning and had lunch near the river. Then we walked around the old city centre.
A: Did you stay overnight?
B: No, we came back on Sunday evening. The train was crowded, but we found seats after about twenty minutes.
A: Sounds like a busy day.
B: It was, but I really enjoyed it.
I visited my aunt last Sunday.
She didn't take the train.
Did you enjoy the exhibition?
They were tired after the trip.
Retell Elena's Saturday in six short steps.

audioSourceTexts: sentence stress distinguishes background from key event
reduced was/were in connected speech
linking in while_I_was / when_I
